source.title: An Emulator for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models using Small Language Models
source.authors: Eric Mitchell; Rafael Rafailov; Archit Sharma; Chelsea Finn; Christopher D. Manning

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how model scale relates to downstream helpfulness and factuality, using emulated fine-tuning rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scale-related downstream evaluations that bear on V6. Its reward-interpolation, speculative-decoding, decoding-ablation, and human-judge-validation results do not test the listed versions. The paper cites scaling-law work, but those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study introduces emulated fine-tuning (EFT) and reports how its emulated mixes of pretraining and fine-tuning scale perform. It compares only two sizes per family (about 7B vs 33–180B). Scores are normalized between the real small and large fine-tuned models, so 'large beats small' is built into the scale rather than measured. It never fits or tests whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss. Its scientific finding is an attribution question (which training stage drives factuality vs helpfulness), not a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that scaling fine-tuning mainly improves helpfulness and scaling pretraining mainly improves factuality. They also find that EFT up-scaling (large base plus small fine-tuned delta) recovers most of the factuality gain of large-scale fine-tuning without training, and that EFT allows test-time helpful-harmless tradeoffs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses emulated fine-tuning to combine base-model probabilities and fine-tuning behavior deltas, and evaluates helpfulness and factuality rather than fitting held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes depend on which stage is scaled: pretraining scale primarily benefits factuality, while fine-tuning scale primarily benefits helpfulness.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling pretraining alone (EFT up-scaling) recovers about 0.67 of the factuality gap but about 0.30 of the helpfulness gap. Scaling fine-tuning alone (down-scaling) recovers about 0.73 of helpfulness and about 0.31 of factuality. These are averages over Llama-1, Llama-2 and Falcon on HH and ELI5 (GPT-4 judged).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling the pretraining stage mainly improves factual accuracy, while scaling the fine-tuning stage mainly improves helpfulness of chat models.

record.problems: The scale experiments use selected model families and two prompt datasets with 256 prompts each. The main results are described largely as normalized trends, with no uncertainty estimates stated for those results in the supplied text. GPT-4 is used as the evaluator for helpfulness and factuality.
record.rows_left_out: Per-family and per-dataset outcomes are presented in Figures 4 and 6, but the supplied text does not provide readable exact values for each plotted result. Those figure-specific rows are omitted rather than assigning values or conditions that cannot be verified from the text.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
Only two scales per family. Scores are normalized to the small and large fine-tuned models. There is no fit or test of a predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream scores.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tests' link and its labels are dropped. The paper does not address whether downstream performance scales predictably, only how two-point emulated combinations fall between fixed small and large endpoints. Figure 3 values (0.73/0.31 down-scaling; 0.30/0.67 up-scaling) are readable from the extracted text, contrary to the record's notes. The Llama-1 large fine-tuned model is Vicuna-33B, not 65B, a mismatch the record's size field omits. Falcon-180B down-scaling used 8-bit inference.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
The study does not fit loss curves on small runs or test predictions on larger runs.
The study does not compare parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
The study does not vary depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
It evaluates helpfulness and factuality across selected scale combinations, but does not fit or test a quantitative predictive relationship between downstream scores and scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law exponents or fitting choices, or test whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.operation_detail: EFT up-scaling: use a large pre-trained model with a small-scale fine-tuning behavior delta

conditions.value: Normalized improvements averaged across Llama-1, Llama-2, and Falcon families and both datasets
Pretraining scale increased while fine-tuning scale remained small

rows.baseline: Small fine-tuned model is normalized to 0.0; large fine-tuned model to 1.0
rows.value: Up-scaling gives significant gains in factuality; the aggregate description says it produces nearly 70% of the factuality gains compared with the small fine-tuned model alone.
rows.note: The nearly 70% figure is an aggregate statement in the paper; no exact per-family or per-dataset scores are stated in the supplied text.
rows.check: Measures EFT up-scaling's normalized factuality gain (0.67 in Figure 3), the study's own method relative to real small and large models. It is not a test of predictable downstream improvement with scale. Value can be stated as 0.67 normalized.
